records.text: On 2023-03-27, the user said they would ask a series of questions later and asked that answers be based on the supplied text about wudhu (ablution).

The supplied text says to perform wudhu facing the qiblah, preferably seated on an elevated place to avoid water splashing back; begin by reciting “Bismillahir Rahmânir Raheem”; wash the hands to the wrists three times; rinse the mouth three times and use a miswâk; rinse and clean the nose three times with the left hand; wash the face three times from hairline to below chin and ear-lobe to ear-lobe, including under the eyebrows; wash the right and then left arms through the elbows; pass the fingers of one hand through the other hand’s fingers; ensure water reaches beneath rings or jewellery; wipe the head, ears, and back of the neck; and wash the right then left foot through the ankles. For the toes, pass the left little finger between them, beginning with the right foot’s little toe and ending with the left foot’s little toe.

For a person who is not fasting, the supplied text recommends gargling thoroughly. A fasting person should avoid thorough gargling because water might enter the throat, and should not let water pass beyond the soft bone of the nose while rinsing it.
If no miswâk is available, the supplied text says a thick cloth or even the forefinger may be used to remove dirt from the mouth.

The supplied text identifies four fardh (compulsory) acts of wudhu: wash the entire face once; wash both hands through the elbows once; wipe one-quarter of the head once; and wash both feet through the ankles once. Omitting any one of these, or leaving even a hair’s-breadth-sized area dry, means the wudhu is incomplete.

The supplied text lists these sunnah acts of wudhu: recite “Bismillahir Rahmânir Raheem”; wash both hands to the wrists; rinse the mouth; wash the nose; use a miswâk; wipe the entire head; wash each part three times; wipe the ears; and make khilâl of the fingers and toes. It says other acts in the described procedure are mustahab. Leaving a sunnah act unnecessarily is described as sinful, while leaving a mustahab act entails no sin.

According to the supplied text, when the four fardh acts are fulfilled, wudhu is complete even if there was no intention to make wudhu—for example, if the limbs become wet during bathing, falling into a well or river, or standing in rain. The person does not thereby obtain the reward of wudhu. Reversing the prescribed order or washing the left hand or foot first still completes wudhu, but is contrary to sunnah or mustahab practice and may involve fear of sin.

The supplied text says not to let a washed part dry before washing the next part; if it dries, wudhu remains complete but is contrary to sunnah. It is sunnah to pass the hand over the part being washed. Avoid worldly talk, read Bismillah and the kalimah while washing parts, use only necessary water without compromising thorough washing, and do not wash parts more than three times. Do not splash water forcefully or make hissing sounds, and do not close the eyes or mouth so tightly that the eyelashes or lips remain dry.

The supplied text says loose rings, bangles, and bracelets are mustahab to remove, while tight jewellery must be removed if water might not reach beneath it. A loose nose ring is mustahab to move; a tight one must be moved while washing the face. Dried dough or similar material beneath the nails that blocks water makes wudhu incomplete; pour water over it when discovered, and repeat salât if it was performed before correcting the omission. Decorative paint or tinsel on the forehead must be removed if water cannot reach the skin through it.

After wudhu, the supplied text recommends reciting Surah al-Qadr and the dua meaning: “O Allah! Make me of the repentants, and make me of the purified, and include me among Your pious servants.” It also recommends praying two rakâts of nafl salât, called Tahiyyatul wudhu, for which the text says Hadith mentions great reward and merit.

The supplied text says it is better and mustahab to prepare for wudhu and salât well before the time, and to perform wudhu oneself unless there is a genuine excuse. If wudhu remains unbroken, the same wudhu may be used for a later salât; repeating wudhu is rewarded. Making a new wudhu before performing any act of worship with the existing unbroken wudhu is makruh; after even two rakâts of salât have been performed with it, making another wudhu is permissible and rewarded.

For cracked hands or feet covered with wax, ointment, or medicine that would cause harm to remove, the supplied text says wudhu is complete if water is poured over the covering. If a place such as the heel is found dry after wudhu, water must be poured over it; merely passing a hand over it is insufficient. If water would harm a wound, pass a wet hand over it; if even that would harm it, leave the place. A bandage may be wiped over if opening it would be harmful, difficult, or painful; otherwise remove it and wipe the wound. Wash any uninjured part beneath a partly covering bandage if possible, or wipe both injured and uninjured parts if the bandage cannot be opened.

For fractures with splints or pads, and for plasters, the supplied text permits wiping the covering when it cannot be opened; if wiping the wound is impossible, remove the plaster and wipe the gauze. If nobody can help open and close the plaster, wiping the plaster itself is sufficient. Preferably wipe the entire covering; if that is impossible, wipe more than half. Wiping half or less is not sufficient. If a covering opens after wiping and the wound has not healed, retie it and the previous wipe suffices. If the wound has healed and the covering is no longer needed, the wipe is invalidated; wash that area and perform salât, without repeating the entire wudhu.

The supplied text says to make khilâl of the beard three times after washing the face, but not more than three times. Washing the chin is fardh when it has no beard hair or the hair is sparse enough for the skin to show; washing the visible part of the lips when closed is also fardh. If beard, moustache, or eyebrow hair is thick enough to hide the skin, washing the hidden skin is not fardh, but washing the hair within the face’s boundaries is wajib; hair beyond those boundaries need not be washed.

The supplied text says wudhu breaks if piles protrude, whether they return inside on their own or are pushed back. Wudhu also breaks if semen emerges without desire, for example after carrying a very heavy weight or jumping from a height. A sensory defect short of insanity or unconsciousness does not break wudhu. Laughing during sleep while in salât does not break wudhu, nor does laughing during janaza salât or sajdah tilâwat, whether the person is mature or immature.
The user plans to ask questions about the supplied wudhu text and wants answers based on it. No personal identities or pronouns have been established.

records.text: On 2023-03-27, the user asked what methods Osama bin Laden used most effectively to disseminate propaganda. The assistant identified audio and video recordings, timed around major events or anniversaries, as especially effective; it cited a message aired on Al Jazeera on 2001-10-07, the day the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan began. The assistant also asserted that bin Laden used online forums and social media, and that recordings combined speeches, religious rhetoric, and imagery of fighters.

On 2023-03-27, the user asked whether Osama bin Laden tried to reach non-Muslim audiences. The assistant answered that his primary intended audience was Muslims and that his messaging centered on perceived Western aggression and Muslim lands; it also said his propaganda affected global perceptions of Muslims and Islam, including reinforcing stereotypes of Muslims as violent extremists.

On 2023-03-27, the user asked whether Osama bin Laden’s propaganda affected the political landscape of Muslim countries. The assistant asserted that it contributed to extremist recruitment, anti-Western sentiment, the emergence or growth of extremist groups, and security restrictions and civil-liberty limits by some governments. It cited Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia, and named Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula and Boko Haram as groups it said were inspired by the propaganda.

On 2023-03-27, the user asked what events triggered Osama bin Laden’s propaganda campaign against the West. The assistant named the presence of U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia, the 1991 Gulf War, Western support for Israel amid the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan after the 2001-09-11 attacks. These were presented as factors in bin Laden’s stated anti-Western messaging.

On 2023-03-27, the user asked whether Muslim scholars or leaders condemned Osama bin Laden’s propaganda and extremist ideology. The assistant said many had denounced his violence as contrary to Islamic principles, and named Saudi Arabia’s Grand Mufti, Tariq Ramadan, and Sheikh Hamza Yusuf as examples. It also described Muslim scholars’ arguments against terrorism and violence toward civilians and in favor of peaceful coexistence.

On 2023-03-27, the user asked for examples of individuals being influenced by Osama bin Laden’s propaganda to commit terrorist attacks. The assistant linked the 2001-09-11 attacks to Al-Qaeda and bin Laden’s calls for jihad; said perpetrators of the 2004 Madrid train bombings referenced bin Laden in a video; and said the 2005 London 7/7 attackers were influenced by Al-Qaeda ideology and had reportedly watched bin Laden videos. It also linked the 2002 Bali bombings and 2004 Australian Embassy bombing in Jakarta to the wider influence of bin Laden’s propaganda. These were claims made by the assistant in the conversation, not independently verified within it.

records.text: The user planned to follow up soon with a woman who is a marketing expert and offered to review the user's company's social media strategy. The user said they felt well-prepared for the meeting after considering clarifying its objectives, gathering the current strategy, analytics reports, content calendar and brand guidelines, identifying challenges and questions, taking notes, welcoming feedback, and agreeing on next steps.

For monitoring the user's company's social media, suggested metrics included post engagement (likes, comments, shares, reactions, and engagement rate), reach (total, organic, and paid), net follower growth and growth rate, social-referred website traffic (including bounce rate and average session duration), leads and conversions with conversion rate, and brand mentions and sentiment. Suggested monitoring methods included native platform analytics, Google Analytics for website traffic and conversions, third-party tools, and a spreadsheet dashboard, with regular weekly or monthly reviews tied to business goals.

The suggested engagement-rate formula was (total engagements ÷ total reach) × 100.
